baslik: Is Going Gluten-Free Healthier Without Celiac Disease?
yorum: Have you ever tried cutting out gluten? If you did, what made you try it, and did you notice a difference?
aciklama_giris:
Gluten-free eating has spread far beyond people with celiac disease. In two large Harvard-linked cohorts, adults without celiac disease who ate less gluten did not have fewer heart attacks, and they had a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Those are associations, not proof of cause, and gluten-free packaged foods often contain less protein and cost far more.

In this video we cover who truly needs a gluten-free diet (celiac disease, wheat allergy and non-celiac gluten sensitivity), what the 26-year heart study and the diabetes study found, what controlled trials say about gluten sensitivity, what gluten-free products actually contain, and why you should get tested before you cut gluten.

sahneler.metin: In one US survey, gluten-free eating among people without celiac disease more than tripled in five years.
sahneler.gorsel: a tall supermarket shelf stacked with boxes of pasta and loaves of bread in plain wrappers, a shopping basket in the foreground
sahneler.etiket: Choung et al. · Mayo Clin Proc · 2017

baslik.not: in five years, among people without celiac disease

sahneler.metin: Then a Harvard study followed 110,000 people for 26 years, and the ones who ate the least gluten had a surprise waiting.
sahneler.gorsel: a long wooden table with two loaves of bread, one whole wheat and one pale, with a red heart symbol standing between them

sahneler.metin: By the end, you'll know who truly needs it, what labels hide, and what to do before cutting gluten.
sahneler.gorsel: a kitchen counter with a sliced whole wheat loaf, a bowl of pasta and a notebook with blank pages, morning light from a window

sahneler.metin: This is The Food Almanac. Let's start with what gluten actually is, and who has a real medical reason to avoid it.
sahneler.gorsel: a sheaf of wheat, barley and rye stalks tied together beside a rustic loaf of bread, in the style of an old botanical plate

sahneler.metin: Three conditions give people a real medical reason to avoid gluten. Let's meet them one at a time.
Gluten is a group of proteins found in wheat, barley and rye. That means it shows up in bread, pasta, cereal and many baked goods, which is why cutting it out changes so much of what's on your plate.
sahneler.gorsel: a bread loaf, a bowl of cooked pasta, a bowl of cereal and a muffin arranged on a wooden table beside a bundle of wheat stalks

sahneler.metin: The first condition is celiac disease, an autoimmune disease. When people with celiac disease eat gluten, their immune system attacks and damages the lining of the small intestine.
sahneler.gorsel: a textbook engraving of the small intestine opened to show finger-like villi along the inner wall, a slice of bread resting beside it

sahneler.metin: The National Institutes of Health estimates that about 2 million people in the United States have celiac disease, and about 1 percent of people worldwide. Many of them have never been diagnosed.
sahneler.gorsel: a crowd of one hundred small identical figures drawn as an engraving, with a single figure at the front standing out
sahneler.etiket: NIDDK · Definition & Facts for Celiac Disease

baslik.not: Americans estimated to have celiac disease

sahneler.metin: A 2018 meta-analysis pooled 96 studies. It found celiac antibodies in 1.4 percent of people worldwide, and biopsy-confirmed disease in 0.7 percent.
sahneler.gorsel: a laboratory bench with a rack of small capped sample tubes, an antique brass microscope and an open notebook with blank pages
sahneler.etiket: Singh et al. · Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol · 2018

sahneler.metin: The second condition is wheat allergy, an immune reaction to wheat. Its symptoms, such as itchy eyes or trouble breathing, differ from celiac disease, and it does not cause long-term damage to the small intestine.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of wheat flour with a wooden scoop and a few wheat kernels scattered on a table, a clean handkerchief beside it

sahneler.metin: The third is non-celiac gluten sensitivity. People get symptoms such as belly pain and tiredness, but they test negative for celiac disease, and their small intestine is not damaged.
sahneler.gorsel: a person's silhouette drawn as a vintage engraving, seated and holding their stomach, a plate of bread and pasta on the table in front of them

sahneler.metin: Notice what's missing from that list: a general reason for everyone else. So the real question is whether cutting gluten helps people who have none of these three. Later, we'll also look at what's inside gluten-free packaged foods.
sahneler.gorsel: a loaf of bread on a wooden board with a knife beside it, a question mark formed by three small wheat kernels on the table

sahneler.metin: In 2017, researchers at Columbia and Harvard asked a direct question. Does long-term gluten intake change the risk of heart disease in people without celiac disease?
They used two huge American cohorts: 64,714 women from the Nurses' Health Study, and 45,303 men from the Health Professionals Follow-up Study. None of them had heart disease when the study began.
sahneler.gorsel: a long rolling hillside of identical small houses in an engraving style, a thin winding road leading toward a distant red heart symbol

baslik.not: no heart disease at the start

sahneler.metin: Every four years, participants filled out a detailed food questionnaire with 131 items. From their answers, the researchers estimated each person's gluten intake, then ranked everyone into five equal groups.
sahneler.gorsel: a hand holding a pencil over a long paper questionnaire with blank lines, a loaf of bread and a bowl of pasta beside it on a desk

sahneler.metin: Then they followed everyone for 26 years, more than two million person-years of follow-up, counting fatal and non-fatal heart attacks. In all, 2,431 women and 4,098 men had one.
sahneler.gorsel: an antique calendar page flipping through many pages, a red heart symbol drawn beside a stack of old paper folders

sahneler.metin: At first glance, the group eating the least gluten looks worse. Their heart disease rate was 352 cases per 100,000 person-years, versus 277 in the group eating the most.

grafik.alt: Raw numbers, before adjusting for lifestyle
grafik.kaynak: Lebwohl et al., BMJ 2017 · 110,017 US adults without heart disease at start · 26 years

sahneler.metin: But that's before accounting for how those groups lived. After adjusting for known risk factors, the difference shrank to almost nothing: a hazard ratio of 0.95, where 1.0 means no difference. The range included no effect at all.
sahneler.gorsel: an antique brass balance scale, level, with a loaf of bread in one pan and a red heart symbol in the other

baslik.not: no clear difference in heart disease risk

sahneler.metin: So the lower raw numbers may not be about gluten itself. When the researchers adjusted for refined grains instead, the highest gluten group had a 15 percent lower risk. The authors read that as a whole grain effect, not a gluten effect.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of brown whole grains beside a bowl of white refined flour, a whole wheat loaf and a pale loaf side by side on a wooden table

sahneler.metin: Their conclusion was careful. Long-term gluten intake was not linked to heart disease, and avoiding gluten may lower whole grain intake, which could matter for the heart. They said gluten-free diets should not be promoted for people without celiac disease.
sahneler.gorsel: a sliced whole wheat loaf on a plate with a red heart symbol drawn above it, a wooden spoon and a small bowl of brown grains beside the plate

sahneler.metin: Remember, this is an observational study. It can show links, not proof of cause. People also reported their own diets, and the participants were nurses and other health professionals, so they may not look like everyone.
sahneler.gorsel: a stack of paper food diaries tied with string on a desk, an antique pen and a pair of round eyeglasses resting on top

sahneler.metin: The same group studied type 2 diabetes in three cohorts totaling about 200,000 US adults. Over 4.24 million person-years of follow-up, 15,947 people developed diabetes.
sahneler.gorsel: a tall stack of paper folders beside a glucose meter with a blank screen, a loaf of bread and a bowl of pasta in the foreground

sahneler.metin: The group eating the most gluten had a 20 percent lower diabetes risk than the group eating the least. After adjusting for cereal fiber, the gap shrank to 13 percent.
sahneler.gorsel: a glucose meter with a blank screen on a table beside a sliced whole wheat loaf and a bowl of brown whole grain cereal

baslik.not: diabetes risk, highest vs lowest gluten fifth

sahneler.metin: Again, that doesn't prove gluten protects anyone. Gluten intake rose together with starch and cereal fiber, and the authors noted that eating less gluten usually means eating less cereal fiber too.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of oat-colored cereal beside a wheat stalk and a thick slice of whole grain bread, a magnified circle showing fibrous grain husk

sahneler.metin: So across two large studies, eating less gluten came with no heart benefit, and with a higher risk of diabetes. Both are associations. But neither supports the idea that gluten-free is healthier for everyone.
sahneler.gorsel: a plain wooden table with a whole wheat loaf at the center, a red heart symbol on one side and a glucose meter with a blank screen on the other

sahneler.bolum: Do some people react to gluten?
sahneler.metin: But plenty of people say gluten makes them feel unwell, even though they don't have celiac disease. Are they imagining it?
No. The symptoms are real. The question researchers ask is what causes them. A team in Australia, led by Jessica Biesiekierski, set out to test whether gluten itself was the trigger.
sahneler.gorsel: an antique laboratory with a bench, a covered tray of bread and muffins and a closed notebook, a tall window with soft light

sahneler.metin: In 2011, they studied 34 adults with irritable bowel syndrome whose symptoms were controlled on a gluten-free diet. For up to six weeks, they ate bread and muffins with gluten, or without, and nobody knew which.
sahneler.gorsel: two identical plates, each with a slice of bread and a muffin, set side by side on a table with a folded cloth between them
sahneler.etiket: Biesiekierski et al. · Am J Gastroenterol · 2011

sahneler.metin: On gluten, 68 percent of people had symptoms that were not adequately controlled. So gluten seemed to matter. But look at the placebo group: 40 percent of them felt worse too, without eating any gluten.
sahneler.gorsel: a bread slice and a muffin on a plate next to an antique scale, two small piles of pebbles in the pans of different heights

baslik.not: symptoms on gluten vs on placebo

sahneler.metin: That is the nocebo effect: when expecting to feel worse can make people feel worse. It doesn't mean the symptoms are faked. It means expectations can shape how the gut feels, and a good trial has to account for that.
sahneler.gorsel: a quiet room with a single armchair, a cup of tea on a small table, a window and a loaf of bread resting on a cloth

sahneler.metin: So in 2013 the same team ran a tighter test in 37 adults who believed they were gluten sensitive. First everyone ate a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain fermentable carbohydrates that can cause gut symptoms.
sahneler.gorsel: a neat row of three bowls holding beans, wheat berries and chopped onion on a wooden counter, a cooking spoon and a loaf of bread behind them

sahneler.metin: Then each person ate three diets for a week apiece: 16 grams of gluten a day, almost no gluten, and a control diet with a different protein. Nobody knew which was which.
sahneler.gorsel: three covered meal trays lined up on a table, a loaf of bread on the first, a bowl of grains on the second and a plain dish on the third

sahneler.metin: Symptoms got worse to a similar degree on gluten and on the control protein. Only 8 percent of participants showed an effect specific to gluten. For most people, gluten itself was not the clear trigger.
sahneler.gorsel: a balance scale with a loaf of bread in one pan and a small bowl of white powder in the other pan, both at the same height

sahneler.metin: Both trials were small, and they involved adults with irritable bowel syndrome, so they can't settle the question for everyone. But the second trial suggests the cause of those symptoms may often be something other than gluten alone.
sahneler.gorsel: a modest research desk with only a few papers with blank pages, a teacup and a magnifying glass resting on a loaf of bread

sahneler.metin: If a food makes you feel unwell, that's worth taking seriously. The right move isn't to guess. It's to find out what's going on with your doctor, and we'll get to exactly how in a moment.
sahneler.gorsel: a doctor's consultation desk with a stethoscope, a closed notebook and a plate holding a slice of bread

sahneler.metin: First, though, there's another reason to be careful about going gluten-free. Look at what's actually inside the box.
A gluten-free label tells you one thing: what's missing. It doesn't tell you whether the food is nutritious. Yet the label can look like a health halo on a grocery shelf.
sahneler.gorsel: a grocery shelf with plain boxes of cookies, crackers and cereal in neat rows, a hand reaching for one box

sahneler.metin: Australian researchers compared the nutrition panels of 3,213 packaged foods from four large supermarkets. They looked at ten food categories, and scored them with a government health star rating.
sahneler.gorsel: a cart in a supermarket aisle filled with boxes of pasta, bread loaves and breakfast cereal, rows of shelves behind it
sahneler.etiket: Wu et al. · Br J Nutr · 2015

sahneler.metin: Gluten-free pasta had 52 percent less protein than regular pasta, and gluten-free bread had 32 percent less. Gluten-free pasta also scored nearly half a star lower on the five star health rating.

grafik.kaynak: Wu et al., Br J Nutr 2015 · 3,213 packaged products, Sydney supermarkets

sahneler.metin: Breads and breakfast cereals showed no significant difference in rating. And the label turned up in surprising places: 87 percent of the processed meats were labeled gluten-free. The authors concluded the products are unlikely to be healthier without a clear need.
sahneler.gorsel: a deli counter with sliced sausages and ham on a wooden board next to a loaf of bread and a bowl of pasta

sahneler.metin: An Austrian study compared 63 gluten-free products with 126 regular counterparts from 12 supermarkets. In 57 percent of the food categories, the gluten-free versions had less than half the protein.
sahneler.gorsel: two shopping baskets side by side on a store floor, one with plain wrapped loaves and pasta and one with slightly different loaves and pasta

sahneler.metin: And the price: gluten-free versions cost between 205 percent more for cereals and 267 percent more for bread and bakery products. That's about three to almost four times the price, in one Austrian study.
sahneler.gorsel: an antique cash register beside a small stack of coins and a loaf of bread on a counter, a tiny balance scale tipped to one side

baslik.not: price of gluten-free bread and bakery products

sahneler.metin: None of this means every gluten-free food is a poor choice. Fruit, vegetables, beans, eggs, fish and plain rice are naturally gluten-free. The trouble is with the packaged substitutes. And for people with celiac disease, those products matter, so some nutrients need attention.
sahneler.gorsel: a market table with fresh vegetables, fruit, a bowl of beans, eggs in a basket and a fillet of fish on a plate

sahneler.metin: Now, the most practical point in this video. If you are thinking about going gluten-free, do this first.

kart.alt: Celiac testing needs gluten in your diet

sahneler.metin: Celiac disease and gluten sensitivity cause overlapping symptoms, so doctors can't tell them apart from symptoms alone. A 2017 review in JAMA says celiac screening should happen before a gluten-free diet starts.
sahneler.gorsel: a doctor's desk with a stethoscope, a clipboard with blank pages and a plate with a slice of bread, a small hourglass beside it

sahneler.metin: The reason is simple. The blood test looks for antibodies that are often higher in untreated celiac disease. The NIH advises not starting a gluten-free diet before testing, because it can affect the results.
sahneler.gorsel: a row of small capped sample tubes in a rack on a laboratory bench, an antique microscope beside a slice of bread on a small plate

sahneler.metin: An expert review from the American Gastroenterological Association makes the same point: cutting out gluten before diagnosis can make the tests less accurate. Doctors then may need you to eat gluten again for a while before testing.
sahneler.gorsel: a simple wooden dinner table set with a plate, a fork and a slice of whole wheat bread, a pocket watch lying beside the plate

sahneler.metin: If you've already gone gluten-free, don't worry. Just tell your doctor, and ask how to be tested. Please don't restart gluten on your own if you have a diagnosed condition. Let your doctor guide you.
sahneler.gorsel: a telephone on a desk beside a calendar with blank squares and a notebook, a pot of tea and a plate with bread on the side

sahneler.metin: A proper diagnosis matters. Many people with celiac disease don't know they have it. And blood tests can also reveal related problems such as anemia, which a doctor can then address.
sahneler.gorsel: a rack of sample tubes beside a stethoscope and a clipboard with blank pages on a clean white table

sahneler.metin: So what should you actually do? Here are four practical steps.
One. If you think gluten bothers you, keep a simple food and symptom diary for two weeks before changing anything. Write down what you ate, and how you felt. Then bring it to your doctor.
sahneler.gorsel: an open notebook with blank lines and a pencil on a kitchen table, a sliced loaf of bread and a cup of tea beside it

sahneler.metin: Two. Ask about celiac testing while you're still eating gluten. If it's negative, you and your doctor can look at other causes, such as irritable bowel syndrome, and decide the next step together.
sahneler.gorsel: a doctor's desk with a stethoscope and a plate with a slice of whole wheat bread, a calendar with blank squares beside them

sahneler.metin: Three. If you do go gluten-free, build your plate from foods that are naturally free of gluten. Vegetables, fruit, beans, eggs, fish, nuts and plain rice, instead of packaged substitutes with less protein and a higher price.
sahneler.gorsel: a dinner plate with grilled fish, steamed vegetables and a scoop of rice, a small bowl of fresh fruit beside it on a wooden table

sahneler.metin: Four. Don't lose your whole grains. If you cut gluten, choose naturally gluten-free whole grains, such as brown rice, quinoa or buckwheat. If you still eat wheat, whole wheat bread is a good way to keep them in.
sahneler.gorsel: three bowls of brown rice, quinoa and buckwheat on a wooden table, a whole wheat loaf at the back

sahneler.metin: And one safety note. If you have diabetes, kidney disease, or take daily medicines, talk to your doctor or dietitian before making big changes to how you eat. A diet trend should never replace treatment.
sahneler.gorsel: a consultation desk with a stethoscope, a closed notebook and a plain pill organizer with empty compartments

sahneler.metin: Let's recap.

kart.alt: Gluten-free is for those who need it

sahneler.metin: Celiac disease, wheat allergy and non-celiac gluten sensitivity are real reasons to avoid gluten. For everyone else, a large Harvard study found no heart benefit from eating less of it.
sahneler.gorsel: the whole wheat loaf from the start, sliced on a wooden board with a red heart symbol standing beside it

sahneler.metin: People who ate the most gluten had a lower diabetes risk, an association partly tied to cereal fiber. And gluten-free packaged foods can have less protein, and cost roughly three times as much or more.
sahneler.gorsel: a supermarket shelf of plain boxed pasta and loaves of bread, a glucose meter with a blank screen on the counter in front

sahneler.metin: Before you cut gluten, get tested for celiac disease while you still eat it. Then build your plate from whole, naturally gluten-free foods, and keep your whole grains in the mix.
sahneler.gorsel: a bright kitchen table with a plate of grilled fish, vegetables and brown rice, a sliced whole wheat loaf at the edge

sahneler.metin: If you found this useful, subscribe to The Food Almanac for more food science, explained calmly and honestly. This video is for education only, and it isn't medical advice. See you in the next one.
